title: RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation as an Agentic Pattern — Audio Guide

chapters.title: Why this is an agentic pattern
chapters.script: Retrieval-augmented generation is the first of three core agentic AI patterns. It feeds a model the specific knowledge it needs at inference time, rather than hoping that knowledge survived pretraining. A pure large language model call is closed world: it can only answer from weights frozen at training time. That works for rephrasing a paragraph, but not for answering what your internal runbook says about a corrupted database. Retrieval-augmented generation turns the model into an open-world agent by giving it a retrieval step before generation. The agent can now consult sources the way a human engineer consults a wiki, a codebase, or a spec. Three things make it agentic rather than just search plus large language model. First, the query is generated, not typed. The model rewrites the user's question into one or more retrieval queries. That rewrite is a decision the agent makes. Second, retrieval is a tool, not a pipeline stage. A capable agent retrieves more than once. It reads, decides whether the result is enough, and may retrieve again with a refined query. This is the bridge into advanced retrieval-augmented generation, which is agentic, multi-hop, and self-correcting. Third, the grounded answer is auditable. Because retrieval is explicit, every claim can be traced back to a source chunk. That is the foundation for evaluations, citations, and hallucination detection.

chapters.title: The core loop
chapters.script: The minimum viable retrieval-augmented generation loop has four steps. First, index your documents offline, once per document. You chunk the document, embed those chunks into vectors, and store the vectors in a vector store. Second, for each user query you retrieve. You embed the user query, then search the vector store for the nearest neighbors, typically the top five. Third, you augment the prompt. You build a prompt that instructs the model to answer using only the sources below, then list the retrieved chunks and the user's question. Fourth, you generate. The large language model produces an answer from that prompt. Every production system is a variation on this loop. The interesting engineering lives in the parameters: how you chunk, which embedding model you pick, how many neighbors you retrieve, how you rerank, and how you compose the final prompt. Each of those has its own article deeper in the knowledge base.

chapters.title: When to add it and when not to
chapters.script: Reach for retrieval-augmented generation when the answer depends on data that is private, recent, or too large to fit in the context window. Examples are internal documents, customer records, last week's news, or a fifty-thousand-file codebase. Also reach for it when you need citations. Regulators, lawyers, and security reviewers all want to see which document a claim came from. And reach for it when the knowledge changes faster than you can fine-tune, which is most enterprise knowledge. Do not reach for retrieval-augmented generation when the question is reasoning over input the user has already pasted. You already have the context, so retrieval adds noise. Also avoid it when you only need style, format, or tone shaping. That is a prompt engineering problem, not a retrieval one. And avoid it when the answer is small, stable, and finite, such as a list of twenty product SKUs. In that case, just inject the list into the system prompt and skip the vector store. A useful smell test: if the same answer should always come from the same source document, retrieval-augmented generation is right. If the answer depends on the user's question and a tool call, you want tool use instead. If the answer should improve as the agent has more conversations, you want memory.

chapters.title: Job-spec context
chapters.script: The trio of retrieval-augmented generation, tool use, and memory appears verbatim in product-engineer job descriptions. For example, the RPM Interactive AI Product Engineer Contract lists this pattern as a hiring requirement. To cover the full bullet, pair this overview with the introductions to tool use and memory.
